items.title: Mercury is liquid for the same reason gold is yellow
items.claim: Mercury (Z=80) is the only metal liquid at room temperature, melting at -39°C. Cadmium just above it melts at 321°C; gold just before it at 1064°C. Mercury's anomaly is, like gold's colour, a consequence of special relativity.
items.prompt: What causes mercury's low melting point?

options.text: Relativistic contraction of mercury's 6s orbital makes its outer electrons less available for metallic bonding, so metallic bonds between Hg atoms are weak — much weaker than in cadmium or zinc

items.reveal:
Mercury has a filled 4f, 5d and 6s subshell. Relativistic contraction pulls the 6s electrons tightly to the nucleus, making them behave more like a noble-gas core than valence electrons.

Metallic bonding relies on delocalised valence electrons forming a 'sea'. With mercury's 6s electrons less willing to delocalise, the lattice is held together more by van der Waals forces and weak metallic interaction — like a giant noble gas.

Without relativistic effects, calculations suggest mercury would melt around 80°C, just like cadmium. The 'special' behaviour of an entire familiar element comes from one of physics' deepest theories.
items.why: Chemistry students treat elements as static atomic-orbital pictures. Heavy elements need relativity to be understood at all.

items.title: pH 1 to pH 2 is a tenfold change, not a small one
items.claim: The pH scale runs from 0 to 14 and looks linear. It isn't. pH is the negative logarithm of [H+]. Each step on the scale is a factor of 10 in hydrogen-ion concentration.
items.prompt: How much more acidic is stomach acid (pH 1) than pure water (pH 7)?
items.reveal:
pH = -log10[H+]. Stomach acid at pH 1 has [H+] = 0.1 M. Pure water at pH 7 has [H+] = 10 to the minus 7 M. The ratio is 10 to the 6 — a million.

This is why diluting a strong acid even tenfold barely changes its pH: the absolute concentration drops by a factor of 10, the pH only shifts by 1 unit.

The same logic applies to the Richter scale (earthquakes), decibels (sound intensity), and stellar magnitudes (brightness). Logarithmic scales let humans handle quantities spanning many orders of magnitude — but they hide the underlying spread.
items.why: Linear-looking scales can describe quantities ranging over 14 orders of magnitude. Acidity's arithmetic must respect the log.

items.title: Push CO2 hard enough and it becomes neither gas nor liquid
items.claim: Above 31.1°C and 73.8 bar, carbon dioxide enters a 'supercritical' state — it fills its container like a gas but has the density and solvent power of a liquid. It is now the standard solvent for decaffeinating coffee.
items.prompt: Why is supercritical CO2 useful for extracting compounds from natural materials?

options.text: It penetrates porous solids like a gas, dissolves organics like a liquid, and can be removed cleanly by depressurisation — leaving no solvent residue
It is the only solvent that dissolves caffeine

items.reveal:
On a pressure-temperature phase diagram, the liquid-gas boundary terminates at a critical point. Beyond it, the distinction between liquid and gas disappears — there is a single fluid phase whose density can be tuned continuously by changing pressure.

For CO2 the critical point is at 31.1°C and 73.8 bar — easily reachable in industrial equipment. Supercritical CO2 dissolves caffeine but not the flavour compounds in coffee beans. After extraction, depressurising vaporises the CO2 instantly with no residue.

Applications: hop extraction for beer, essential oil isolation, dry cleaning, semiconductor cleaning, dyeing textiles without water, and recently as a working fluid in highly efficient power-cycle generators.
items.why: Phase diagrams in GCSE end at the liquid-gas boundary. The fluid beyond the critical point has properties of both — and quietly underpins major industries.
